newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition fears being cheated of election win.
newsitem.headline: Opposition fears being cheated of election win.

text.p: Tensions rose across Serbia as thousands of opposition supporters demonstrated in the city of Nis on Tuesday fearing the authorities would resort to massive fraud in local elections results to deny them victory.

Nis was among several cities, including the capital Belgrade, where the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition claimed to have swept the ruling Socialists and their allies from power according to unofficial results from Sunday's vote.

The scale of the defeat apparently stunned the Socialist Party (SPS) led by President Slobodan Milosevic and prompted immediate concern that attempts would be made to overturn it when official results are announced on Tuesday evening.

Zajedno leaders organised a protest rally at the city hall in Nis, an important industrial centre 200 km (125 km) south of Belgrade, on Tuesday after local supporters said election officials were annulling opposition victories.
The rally was one of the biggest ever held in Nis, independent Belgrade radio 92 reported.
Witnesses said up to 50,000 people have gathered in the city center waiting for official results due at 1900 GMT.

It said the town election commission has cancelled results from as many as 19 polling stations. Results were also cancelled in the towns of Smederevska Palanka, Jagodina, Pancevo and others, the radio said.

"The SPS throughout Serbia is trying to annul election results by falsifying election records and lodging complaints," the Democratic Party, one of the Zajedno allies, said in a statement faxed to Reuters.
"The Socialists simply cannot admit their defeat and are trying to provoke disturbances and demonstrations throughout the country," the Democratic Party said.
Opposition leaders appealed to police and army commanders in the town to help ensure the opposition was not cheated of its biggest electoral success of the Milosevic era.
Tensions were also rising in Kraljevo, Ljiljana Radonjic, a Democratic Party spokeswoman in the central Serbian town told Reuters.
She feared mass assembly could easily run out of control and turn into open riots.
Opposition leaders on hunger strike inside the city hall building are receiving a flood of offers for assistance from surrounding towns, she said.
The Socialist coalition, which won a comfortable victory in federal parliamentary elections this month, claimed to have captured 134 out of 174 municipalities in Serbia.
But the loss of the major cities, where industrial unrest against poverty and joblessness has recently increased, would be a severe blow to the Socialists' prestige.
Analysts said voters appeared to have voted one way in the federal elections in order to keep Milosevic in power and another in the municipal poll to rein in his Socialists.
In Belgrade, opposition leaders held a celebration in the city centre on Monday night before marching to city hall to meet the head of the Belgrade electoral commission.
Vuk Draskovic, head of the Serbian Renewal Movement, also part of the Zajedno coalition, warned the commission not to tamper with the results.
The commission's legal obligation was to announce results by Tuesday night at the latest.
Draskovic warned that the opposition would "defend" its victory, hinting at possible street demonstrations to force authorities to recognise election results.
In 1991, he led protests against state control of the media which Milosevic crushed with tanks after two men were killed.
Apart from Belgrade, towns claimed by the opposition included Nis, Kragujevac, Uzice, Kraljevo, Kikinda, Zrenjanin and Cacak, and Novi Sad, the provincial capital of Vojvodina.

Yugoslav voters have been reluctant to trust the opposition, preferring to stay with Milosevic who wields complete control over the press, army, police and national administration as well as the country's purse strings.
Political sources said the Socialist-led government had more than enough power to frustrate opposition-controlled municipal councils and make them look inept.
But Milosevic, seeking a new post-war political consensus, has flirted with Draskovic and other opposition leaders before.
Throwing them control of a few large towns could presage the gradual formation of a new centrist bloc with Milosevic in alliance with the moderate opposition.
